profiles.title: The Tikhvin Icon of the Mother of God
profiles.subject: Theotokos

overview.text: The Tikhvin icon belongs to the Hodegetria family of Mother-and-Child images. Archpriest John Matusiak’s account combines its Russian monastic history, accounts of miracles and its twentieth-century preservation outside Russia.
overview.reason: Necessary concise account of a modern published source; substantial verbatim reproduction is not licensed. This is an editorial summary, not the source author’s wording.

blocks.text: Matusiak identifies a distinguishing detail: the Christ child’s legs are crossed and the sole of a foot faces the viewer. The Virgin’s pose relates it to Hodegetria images such as the Iveron icon, while the child’s feet help distinguish this particular composition.
blocks.reason: Necessary concise account of a modern published source; substantial verbatim reproduction is not licensed. This is an editorial summary, not the source author’s wording.

blocks.text: The source explicitly labels the attribution to Saint Luke as ancient tradition. It relates an appearance above Lake Ladoga in 1383 and the icon’s settling near Tikhvin. During the Second World War it was taken from the monastery; Bishop John Garklavs brought it to the United States in 1949.

blocks.text: The account links the icon with the protection of the monastery during Swedish attacks in 1613–14 and with later venerated copies. It reports that the 2003 pilgrimage began its journey back to Russia; that passage describes the journey at its beginning.
